documents: Smirnov et al. 2022, Izvestiya, Physics of the Solid Earth 58(3):364-378, published paper (PDF)

entry.evidence: From this standpoint, it is interesting to examine the b-value variations during seasonal fluctuations of seismic activity

steps.action: Recall the authors' earlier finding from the earthquake catalog: seasonal seismicity is minimal in May-June and has fall, winter and spring peaks, read as immediate and delayed responses to water-level change.
steps.quote: During the rest of the year, the seismicity has three peaks

steps.action: Pose the question of how the b-value behaves within the seasonal cycle of reservoir-triggered seismicity, noting that no special studies of it exist.
steps.quote: We have not found any special studies of the b-value in the seasonal seismicity variations caused by reservoir operations

steps.action: Select the MERI catalog, with M3+ events from 1983 to 2015 (596 events), to keep the magnitude of completeness homogeneous.
steps.quote: we selected the catalog events with magnitudes starting from 3.0 and chose the time interval from 1983 to 2015

steps.action: Design a superposed-epoch composite annual catalog that folds 33 years into one year, and exclude 1999, 2000 and 2005 because of aftershock sequences (512 events remain).
steps.quote: we used the superposed epoch analysis procedure

steps.action: Estimate the seismicity rate and the upper- and lower-bound b-values in moving windows over the composite year with a modified maximum-likelihood method that corrects for right censoring (Fig. 2).
steps.quote: The upper- and lower-bound estimates of the b-value were calculated using the modified maximum likelihood method

steps.action: Generate 10000 synthetic catalogs (Poisson times with a seasonally varying rate, constant b = 1.4, 512 events), process them identically, and find no artifactual rate-b correlation and relative errors that match the asymptotic MLE errors.
steps.quote: statistical modeling was performed on random synthetic catalogs

steps.action: Compare the real seasonal b-value variations with the constant-b synthetic null: they exceed the one-sigma band but stay within the two-sigma band (Fig. 3).
steps.quote: seasonal variations in the b-value estimated from the real catalog go beyond the one-sigma interval

steps.action: Adopt the published interpretations of the rate maxima: an immediate response from pore-space compression and a delayed response from pore-pressure diffusion, with Gupta's unloading hypothesis named as an alternative.
steps.quote: The maximum in February–March is considered as a delayed response.

steps.action: Read Fig. 2: the two b-value minima (October, March) coincide with the immediate and delayed seismicity maxima; the two b-value maxima fall in phases of water-level rise and fall.
steps.quote: The minima in October and March are approximately concurrent with the months of the maxima in the seasonal seismic activity

steps.action: State two candidate associations for the b-value maxima: the phase of seismic activity or the cycle of water-level (pore-pressure) fluctuations.
steps.quote: it is not clear whether the times of the maxima in the b-value should be correlated to the pattern of changes in seismic activity

steps.action: Design a laboratory analog: a granite sample from the Koyna-Warna KBH05 well, with cyclic pore-pressure increases and decreases shaped like the reservoir water-level curve.
steps.quote: The tested granite sample KBH-5-548-1 was taken from a depth of 548 m from the Phansavale well

steps.action: Set the conditions: 10 MPa confining pressure, preload to 100 MPa then 90 MPa, water injection that forms a macrofracture, then two series of three pore-pressure cycles (1 and 2 MPa) at constant axial strain rate.
steps.quote: The experiment was conducted at constant confining pressure of 10 MPa.

steps.action: Find the acoustic-array catalog too small for statistics and switch to a more sensitive sensor in the press punch, using the uncalibrated energy class K = 2 log A.
steps.quote: However, the size of the acoustic catalog proved to be insufficient for statistical analysis.

steps.action: Build composite AE catalogs per series by superposed epochs and estimate AE rate and b-value in windows of 120 events shifted by 20 (Fig. 6).
steps.quote: For each series of the three cycles of increasing and decreasing pore pressure, we compiled a composite catalog of AE events.

steps.action: Check the superposed-epoch premise: magnitude-frequency graphs of the individual cycles have similar shape and slope to one another and to the composite (Fig. 5).
steps.quote: have a similar shape and a close slope

steps.action: Compare lab with field: the minimum b-value falls near the AE maximum at peak pore pressure, and b-value maxima fall in the pressure rise and decrease phases, as in the field.
steps.quote: the minimum b-value falls approximately on the maximum activity

steps.action: Compare the two lab series (1 and 2 MPa): both show two maxima and one minimum, but the second maximum falls on different segments and the second series has an extra minor maximum.
steps.quote: It is not yet clear whether the difference of the b-value peculiarities in the first and second series is natural or accidental.

steps.action: Set the b-minimum-at-activity-maximum result beside earlier fluid-driven swarm, laboratory and transient-seismicity generalizations from the authors' group.
steps.quote: this effect is characteristic of transient regimes ovberall

steps.action: Acknowledge that the lab does not mimic the two natural pore-pressure mechanisms and restrict the lab-field comparison to the immediate response, where pore pressure is assumed to follow water level.
steps.quote: cannot be directly compared with the complex dynamics of the delayed response in the natural in situ conditions

steps.action: Compare the immediate-response interval (Fig. 7) with the lab: a slight b-value rise followed by a larger drop as activity intensifies, matching the avalanche-unstable crack-coalescence scenario.
steps.quote: the b-value varies (Fig. 7) similarly to the b-value variations observed in the laboratory experiment (Fig. 6)

steps.action: Keep the conclusions: b-value varies regularly over the annual cycle, with minima at both response maxima and maxima in the rise and fall phases, and the lab shows similar patterns.
steps.quote: The minimum b-values fall in the intervals of the maxima in both the immediate and delayed seismic responses.

end.claim: Within the annual cycle of Koyna-Warna reservoir-triggered seismicity (M3+, 1983-2015 composite), the b-value has minima at the immediate and delayed seismicity maxima and maxima during water-level rise and fall phases.

decisive_move.sentence: The superposed-epoch composite catalog with moving-window maximum-likelihood b-value estimation is what makes the intra-annual b-value pattern visible at all, given only 18 M3+ events per year.

gates.evidence: The field data were an existing catalog not acquired for this hypothesis. The laboratory experiment was designed to decide whether b-value maxima follow seismicity or the pore-pressure cycle (p. 369-371). The field pattern was tested against a constant-b synthetic null and lies between one and two sigma (p. 368). No pre-specified analysis or threshold is reported.

imports.item: Poisson point-process synthetic catalogs with exponential magnitude distribution (Monte Carlo null)
Maximum-likelihood estimation corrected for right censoring
Acoustic emission recording during triaxial loading with pore-pressure control

novelty_claims.quote: We have not found any special studies of the b-value in the seasonal seismicity variations caused by reservoir operations
fine features have been identified in the behavior of seasonal components of the reservoir-triggered seismicity

limits: No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The field b-value variations are significant only between one and two sigma against a constant-b null (p. 368), and they rest on one composite year built from about 512 events. The laboratory part is a pilot on one granite sample with two series that differ in detail and an uncalibrated AE sensor (p. 371). The authors state that mapping lab cycles onto both immediate and delayed responses is unproven (p. 373). Sub-claims: (a) the correspondence of lab and field patterns is best_explanation at most, restricted to the immediate response; (b) consistency of the immediate response with the avalanche-unstable fracture scenario is best_explanation (p. 374-375). Inference: the choices of window size, magnitude cutoff and excluded years were probably fixed after inspecting the data; the paper does not say. The rival associations for the b-value maxima are not tested with distinct quantitative predictions.

disagreements.target: Mallika et al. (2013), b-value decreases before M4+ earthquakes in the Koyna-Warna loading phase
disagreements.support: The paper notes that the earlier study left the nature of the loading-phase b-value effect undiscussed, and offers a seasonal b-value pattern tied to pore-pressure responses.
disagreements.quote: The question about the nature of the revealed effect is not discussed.

disagreements.target: Standard asymptotic confidence intervals for MLE b-value on small samples
disagreements.support: Stochastic modeling on synthetic catalogs shows the asymptotic errors match the direct estimates for samples of 40-50 events.
disagreements.quote: the standard confidence intervals based on the asymptotic estimates may not be quite correct
